title: yang — the one that
pattern: noun + yang + description · yang + description (the … one) · Yang mana?
explanation: yang links a noun to a description of it, like who, which or that in English: orang yang tinggal di sebelah (the person who lives next door), kamar yang ada AC-nya (the room with air-con). Leave out the noun and yang … means 'the … one': Saya mau yang merah (I'd like the red one), Yang ini atau yang itu? To ask which one, say Yang mana? A single describing word needs no yang (rumah besar, a big house); adding it picks one out from the others: rumah yang besar, the big house, not the small one.
natural: Pointing at things in a shop or at a warung: Yang ini, ya. Yang pedas atau yang tidak? It also comes before paling for 'the most': yang paling murah, the cheapest one.
stiff: English can drop 'that' (the book I bought), but Indonesian always keeps yang: buku yang saya beli. And don't put yang before every describing word: kopi yang panas sounds as if you're setting it against a cold one, so for plain description say kopi panas.

gap.why: With no noun, yang pedas means 'the spicy one'; itu and ini can't stand in for 'the' here.

examples.registerNotes: At a warung with two kinds of sambal or two versions of a dish, point and say Yang pedas, ya.

gap.why: Yang mana? asks which one; di mana? would ask where.

examples.registerNotes: Said looking along a street or at a photo. Ibu is the polite 'you' for an older woman.

examples.indonesian: Orang yang tinggal di sebelah ramah sekali.
examples.english: The person who lives next door is really friendly.

gap.why: A 'who' that describes someone is yang; siapa only asks a question.

examples.pitfallNote: English speakers reach for siapa (who) here, but siapa only asks questions: orang siapa tinggal … doesn't work.

examples.indonesian: Baju yang saya beli kemarin kekecilan.
examples.english: The top I bought yesterday is too small.

gap.why: English can drop 'that' (the top I bought); Indonesian keeps yang.

examples.pitfallNote: Keep yang even where English leaves 'that' out: without it, baju saya reads as 'my top'. Kekecilan is 'too small' (from kecil).
